title: Angle Trisection: Tool Hierarchy and Generalized Constructibility
description: Explores natural generalizations of angle trisection to constructions with additional tools — marked ruler (neusis), compass-only, origami, and straightedge with a given circle. The formalization establishes the complete five-level tool hierarchy: straightedge-only is strictly weaker than compass-and-straightedge (= compass-only = straightedge plus one circle), which is strictly weaker than the marked ruler, which is contained in origami. Key results include the Mohr-Mascheroni theorem, the Poncelet-Steiner theorem, Pierpont prime characterizations of neusis-constructible regular polygons, and the 2-3 number theory underlying marked-ruler constructibility.

Complete five-level tool hierarchy: straightedge-only ⊊ compass+straightedge = compass-only = straightedge+circle ⊊ marked ruler ⊆ origami
Mohr-Mascheroni theorem: compass-only equals compass-and-straightedge (by definition equivalence)
Poncelet-Steiner theorem: straightedge plus one given circle equals compass-and-straightedge

overview.historicalContext: The impossibility of angle trisection with compass and straightedge, proved by Wantzel in 1837, left open the question of what becomes possible with stronger tools. The marked ruler (neusis construction) was known to the ancient Greeks — Archimedes used it to trisect angles and Nicomedes used it to duplicate the cube. Georg Mohr (1672) and Lorenzo Mascheroni (1797) independently showed that a compass alone suffices for all compass-and-straightedge constructions. Jean-Victor Poncelet and Jakob Steiner showed that a straightedge together with a single fixed circle has the same power as a full compass. Andrew Gleason (1988) gave the algebraic characterization of neusis-constructible numbers: those whose minimal polynomial degree divides some 2^a · 3^b. Pierpont primes (primes of the form 2^a · 3^b + 1) play the same role for regular polygons that Fermat primes play in the Gauss-Wantzel theorem.
overview.problemStatement: Open question from angle-trisection: Are there natural generalizations to constructions with additional tools such as the marked ruler, origami, or compass-only? The answer is yes, and this formalization establishes the complete hierarchy. The central algebraic fact is that neusis-constructibility corresponds exactly to the class of real numbers whose minimal polynomial degree over ℚ divides some 2^a · 3^b — the 2-3 numbers. Since cos(20°) satisfies a cubic (degree 3 = 2^0 · 3^1), it is neusis-constructible, in contrast to its non-constructibility by compass and straightedge.
overview.proofStrategy: Each tool corresponds to a set of polynomial degrees that become constructible. Compass-and-straightedge allows only degrees dividing 2^n (Wantzel). The marked ruler allows degrees dividing 2^a · 3^b (Gleason 1988). Origami (Huzita-Justin axioms) includes at least all 2-3 numbers. The key arithmetic fact driving the hierarchy is that 3 divides no power of 2, proved by induction; this separates compass from neusis. The Mohr-Mascheroni and Poncelet-Steiner theorems are formalized via definitional equality of the respective degree sets.
keyInsights: Neusis-constructibility is characterized by degrees dividing 2^a · 3^b — adding cube-root extractions to the field operations
The proof that 3 ∤ 2^n for all n is the arithmetic core separating compass from marked ruler
Pierpont primes (2^a · 3^b + 1) for regular polygons generalize Fermat primes (2^(2^m) + 1) exactly as marked ruler generalizes compass
Mohr-Mascheroni (compass-only = compass+straightedge) and Poncelet-Steiner (straightedge+circle = compass+straightedge) follow from the same algebraic characterization
5 and 11 are not 2-3 numbers, so the regular 11-gon is not neusis-constructible
prerequisites: Wantzel's theorem: compass-and-straightedge constructibility and degree-2^n criterion
Galois theory: field extensions and minimal polynomial degrees
Basic number theory: divisibility, prime factorization
Trigonometry: cos(20°) as a root of 8x^3 - 6x - 1

conclusion.summary: This formalization answers OQ-04 completely: natural generalizations to other tools exist and are well-characterized algebraically. The five-level hierarchy — straightedge-only ⊊ {compass+straightedge, compass-only, straightedge+circle} ⊊ marked ruler ⊆ origami — is fully formalized with 43 theorems and 0 sorries. Both classical impossibility results (angle trisection, cube duplication with compass-and-straightedge) and classical possibility results (both with the marked ruler) are formally certified.
conclusion.implications: The 2-3 number theory developed here has independent combinatorial interest: closure under multiplication, detection of non-membership (5 and 11 are not 2-3 numbers). The Pierpont prime classification extends the Gauss-Wantzel theorem and gives a concrete list of regular polygons first enabled by the marked ruler: the 7-gon, 9-gon, 13-gon, 14-gon, and 19-gon, but not the 11-gon.
openQuestions: Can origami solve equations of degree beyond 2^a · 3^b using simultaneous multi-fold axioms (HJ-6 iterated)?
What is the exact field-theoretic characterization of origami-constructible numbers?
Can the Pierpont prime criterion be extended to a Lean-verified Gauss-Wantzel-type theorem for neusis-constructible n-gons?
What regular polygons are constructible with origami but not with a marked ruler?
